title: Decision-Based Adversarial Attacks: Reliable Attacks Against Black-Box Machine Learning Models
authors: Wieland Brendel, Jonas Rauber, Matthias Bethge

pages.title: Attacking a model you can barely see
pages.subtitle: The decision-based threat model

blocks.html: Imagine you want to fool a face-recognition gate, a content-moderation filter, or a fraud detector. In a research paper you would be handed the model's gradients and could compute exactly which pixels to nudge. In the real world you get almost nothing: you upload an image and the system replies with a single word — accepted or rejected, cat or dog. No probabilities, no confidence, no internal weights. This paper asks the uncomfortable question: is even that one word enough to break the model? The answer is yes.
The authors organize attacks into three tiers by how much information the attacker is granted. Understanding this ladder is the key to the whole black-box-attack literature.

rows: Only if you own the model

blocks.html: Decision-based is the harshest and most realistic of the three. The paper's contribution is the Boundary Attack: a remarkably simple algorithm that, using only those one-word answers, finds adversarial perturbations as small as those found by strong white-box attacks like Carlini & Wagner.
The core difficulty: the only thing the model tells you is which side of the decision boundary you are on. Everything else must be inferred by repeatedly probing that boundary.

pages.title: What 'hard-label / decision-based' means
pages.subtitle: The shared setup for this whole family of attacks

blocks.html: Every paper in this collection — Boundary Attack, OPT, Sign-OPT, HopSkipJump — lives in the same world, so it is worth nailing down once. In the hard-label (= decision-based) setting the attacker may feed the model any input $x$ and receives back only the predicted class label $c(x)$. That is it. You learn exactly one bit of structure per query: is this point classified the way I want, or not?

Contrast this with the score-based setting, where a query returns a real-valued probability vector. There you can tell whether a tiny change made the model slightly more or less confident, which is almost a numerical gradient. In the hard-label setting that signal is gone: the output is a flat step function that jumps only when you cross the decision boundary (the surface where the predicted class changes). Almost every small change leaves the label untouched and tells you nothing.

Reading this term by term: $c(x)$ is the model's predicted label for input $x$; $y_{\text{orig}}$ is the true class of the clean image; $y_{\text{target}}$ is a class the attacker wants the model to output. An untargeted attack just needs any wrong label; a targeted attack must hit one specific chosen label. Both conditions are checkable with a single query — that is the only handle the attacker has.

Because every query costs money, latency, or risks tripping an anomaly detector, the natural success metric for this entire family is queries-to-success: how many model evaluations are needed to drive the perturbation size (usually the $\ell_2$ norm) below some small threshold. A good attack finds a tiny, often imperceptible perturbation while spending as few queries as possible. Keep that metric in mind — it is the scoreboard every later paper competes on.

items: Boundary Attack (this paper): random-walk along the boundary. Reliable but query-hungry ($10^5$–$10^6$).
OPT: reframe as a smooth optimization over directions; use binary search + zeroth-order gradients.
Sign-OPT: realize you only need the sign of the directional derivative — far cheaper.
HopSkipJump: estimate the gradient direction at the boundary by Monte-Carlo sampling. State-of-the-art query efficiency.

pages.title: Start adversarial, then shrink
pages.subtitle: The defining idea, inverted from the usual recipe

blocks.html: Here is the one idea that makes the Boundary Attack work, and it runs backwards from intuition. Gradient attacks start from the clean image and push it toward the boundary until it just barely flips. The Boundary Attack instead starts from an image that is already adversarial but with a huge, obvious perturbation. It then walks that point along the decision boundary, step by tiny step, shrinking the distance back toward the original image.

Concretely, how do you get an initial adversarial image for free? For an untargeted attack, sample pure uniform noise — a TV-static image — until the model happens to misclassify it (usually instant, since random noise is rarely the true class). For a targeted attack, just grab any real image that the model already labels as the target class. Either way you begin far from the original but safely on the adversarial side.

Why is this clever? Because staying adversarial is trivial to check with a single hard-label query, the entire hard problem collapses to one question: given that I must remain adversarial, how do I get geometrically closer to the original image? No gradients, no scores, no surrogate models.

blocks.text: Two competing objectives at every step

items: Stay on the adversarial side of the boundary — the hard constraint, verified by one query.
Reduce the $\ell_2$ distance to the original clean image — the quantity being minimized.

blocks.html: Boundary Attack: begin with a large adversarial perturbation, then random-walk along the decision boundary to shrink it down toward the original image.

pages.title: A constrained random walk
pages.subtitle: How each proposal step is built

blocks.html: Each iteration proposes a small perturbation $\eta^{k}$ built in two parts, then accepts it only if a single hard-label query confirms the new point is still adversarial. Think of it as surfing a curved surface: a sideways move to explore, then a small step downhill to bank progress.

blocks.tex: \tilde{x}^{k} = x^{k-1} + \eta^{k}, \qquad \eta^{k} \text{ chosen so that } \tilde{x}^{k} \text{ stays adversarial}

blocks.html: Reading term by term: $x^{k-1}$ is the current adversarial point; $\eta^{k}$ is the proposed move; $\tilde{x}^{k}$ is the candidate. The candidate is kept (becomes $x^{k}$) only if $c(\tilde{x}^{k})$ confirms it is still misclassified, otherwise it is discarded and we try again.

blocks.text: The three constraints on each proposal

items: Box constraint: the candidate must remain a valid image (pixels in $[0,255]$ or $[0,1]$).

Orthogonal / spherical move: $\eta^{k}$ is first drawn from a Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, then rescaled and re-projected so the candidate sits on the sphere of the current distance around the original image. This is a sideways slide along the boundary that does not change the distance — pure exploration.
Source step: after the orthogonal move, take a small step toward the original image, which actually shrinks the $\ell_2$ distance. This is where progress is harvested.

blocks.tex: \eta^{k} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \quad \text{then project onto sphere of radius } \lVert x^{k-1} - o \rVert_2 \text{ around original } o

blocks.html: Here $o$ is the original clean image and $\lVert x^{k-1} - o\rVert_2$ is the current perturbation size. Projecting the Gaussian noise back onto that sphere guarantees the exploratory move keeps the distance fixed; only the deliberate inward source step is allowed to reduce it. Splitting exploration (sideways) from progress (inward) is what keeps the walk stable.
The boundary is treated as a surface to surf. Random sideways moves explore it; small inward moves harvest the progress; the single hard-label query is the only referee.

pages.title: Keeping the walk efficient
pages.subtitle: Adaptive step sizes, the only real hyperparameters

blocks.html: The two step magnitudes are the only knobs, and the attack tunes them itself on the fly using acceptance rates — the same trick used in Trust-Region and Markov-Chain Monte Carlo methods. The logic is intuitive: if your steps keep getting rejected, you are stepping too far; if they all succeed, you are being timid and could go bigger.

items: Orthogonal step $\delta$ controls how aggressively we explore the boundary surface. Tuned to keep the acceptance rate near a target of about 50% — shrink it if too few proposals survive, grow it if nearly all do.

Source step $\epsilon$ controls how aggressively we move toward the original. Tuned so roughly a quarter of proposals still land adversarial; if pushing inward keeps flipping us back, $\epsilon$ is reduced.
Both decay over time, so the attack naturally refines a coarse solution into a fine one, asymptotically hugging the boundary.

blocks.html: This self-tuning is why the method is described as hyperparameter-light and reliable: there is essentially nothing to grid-search. The same code, untouched, works on MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet, and on defended or non-differentiable models where gradient estimates would be meaningless.

Design rationale: an MCMC-style accept/reject walk is the natural fit for a setting where the only feedback is a binary in/out signal. You cannot do gradient descent on a step function, but you can do a guided random walk on one. The genius is that the constraint (stay adversarial) and the objective (get closer) are decoupled into the two step types, so neither fights the other.

The headline result: using only hard labels, the Boundary Attack finds adversarial perturbations whose $\ell_2$ size is competitive with the strongest white-box attacks, including the Carlini & Wagner $\ell_2$ attack and DeepFool, on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet (VGG-19, ResNet-50, Inception-v3). That a labels-only attacker matches a full-gradient attacker was the paper's shock value.

The honest catch is query cost. Because each step extracts at most one bit, reaching very small perturbations can take on the order of $10^5$ to $10^6$ queries. This single weakness became the explicit research target of everything that followed — OPT, Sign-OPT, and HopSkipJump are all, in effect, answers to 'can we extract more than one bit per query?'

Crucially, the attack transfers to real, defended, and non-differentiable systems. The authors demonstrate it against models with gradient masking (a defense that deliberately hides or obfuscates gradients) and against commercial black-box classifiers from Clarifai, where gradient and transfer attacks fail outright. It needs no substitute model, no surrogate gradients, and no access to training data.

The Boundary Attack established that the strictest threat model — labels only — is genuinely dangerous, not an academic curiosity. It set the template the rest of this family refines: treat the decision boundary as the object of study, and minimize distance to it using only label queries.

A common misconception it dispelled: that hiding gradients or scores makes a model safe. Gradient masking defenses looked strong against white-box attacks precisely because they broke gradients — but the Boundary Attack never uses gradients, so masking does nothing to it. This foreshadowed the later Obfuscated Gradients paper, which argued that many published defenses give a false sense of security.

The lineage from here is direct: OPT reformulates the search as a smooth optimization over attack directions; Sign-OPT shows you only need the sign of the directional derivative, slashing the per-direction query cost; HopSkipJump estimates the gradient direction at the boundary by Monte-Carlo sampling and reaches state-of-the-art query efficiency. Each can be read as one more bite out of the Boundary Attack's query bill.
The lasting lesson: an attacker who can only see the final decision is still a serious threat. Security through opacity of scores and gradients is not security.
